title: The Modern Devotion
hookLine: Dutch lay communities practice simple inner prayer; the Imitation of Christ comes from them

lines: FROM THE OUTSIDE TO THE INSIDE.
cards: Nobody in this narrow house in a Dutch town wears a habit. Nobody has taken vows. It's late in the middle ages.
The men copy books by hand for a living, pool what they earn, eat at one table, and pray. Down the street, a house of women does much the same, sewing and spinning.
On Sunday they all walk to the parish church like their neighbors. What sets them apart is quieter: they're trying to let the faith travel from the outside of their lives to the inside.
The movement came to be called the Modern Devotion.

teach.h: GEERT GROOTE AND THE COMMON LIFE.
teach.b: Start with the man tradition puts at the root: Geert Groote, a preacher from Deventer who left a comfortable career and called people back to a plain, interior faith.
Around him, laymen and laywomen began living together as the Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life, and others became canons in religious houses linked to the movement. Next, the method.

teach.h: READ A LITTLE, SLOWLY. KEEP ONE LINE.
teach.b: Read a little Scripture, slowly. Copy out a line that strikes you, keep it close, and return to it through the day. Look honestly at your own heart at night.
No ladders of mystical stages; just an ordinary day, turned toward God. Then, the book.
From these communities came The Imitation of Christ, which tradition attributes to Thomas à Kempis, a canon of one of their houses.
It opens with Jesus's words from John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness." Then it turns inward again and again.
Early on it says, in effect, that a humble knowledge of yourself is a surer road to God than deep learning. Finally, the direction: inward.

teach.h: THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS WITHIN YOU.
teach.b: In Luke, Jesus says, "the kingdom of God is within you."
The Modern Devotion took him at his word. Not instead of the Mass and the sacraments; they kept those. Underneath them.
Copyists, weavers, schoolmasters, with ordinary jobs, doing one quiet thing on purpose every day.

how: Catholics still read The Imitation of Christ, often a chapter or a few lines at a time, and some keep it beside the Bible for daily spiritual reading or use it in retreats.

o: a reform that replaced the Mass with Bible reading
a new style of church music in the Renaissance
a lay movement of plain, inward prayer

games.q: you're a young copyist in a Dutch town. you want to live your faith more deeply, but you have a trade and no call to the cloister. what do you do?
o: leave your trade and join a strict monastery.
share a house, work and prayer with others, and keep your trade.
decide deep faith is for priests and nuns, and leave it to them.
games.why: the Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life did just this: ordinary work, a shared table, and simple inward prayer.

practice: Choose one short line, and today's will do: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness.
Say it once, slowly, in your head, and when your mind drifts to the dishes or the inbox, don't scold it; come back to the line the way you'd turn back to a friend after a car horn.
If you pray, let the line become your prayer; if not, let it be a place to rest.

wordCard.voice: Modern Devotion. Lay communities in the Low Countries who practiced plain, inward prayer, and from whom The Imitation of Christ came. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the modern devotion, the name the movement was given.

carryVoice: Your line: inward. An ordinary day can be turned toward God from the inside. Day eight hundred twenty-eight, done.
